stem: A 45-year-old man is evaluated for worsening polyuria and polydipsia.  BMI is 33 kg/m2.  Hemoglobin A1c is >10%.  He is prescribed a medication that alters glucose metabolism by increasing the concentration of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate within hepatocytes.  A high intracellular concentration of this metabolite is most likely to inhibit which of the following metabolic processes?​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌
explanation:
This patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus (eg, obesity, polyuria, polydipsia, hemoglobin A1c >10%) has most likely been prescribed insulin, which is often initiated in patients with marked, symptomatic hyperglycemia.  In hepatocytes, insulin stimulates the production of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F26BP), a critical regulator of glycolysis/gluconeogenesis.

F26BP levels are controlled by a bifunctional enzyme with both a kinase domain (phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate) and a phosphatase domain (dephosphorylates F26BP).  Insulin promotes dephosphorylation of the enzyme, which activates the kinase domain (phosphofructokinase-2) and inhibits the phosphatase domain (fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase), increasing conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to F26BP.  Glucagon promotes phosphorylation of the enzyme, which has the opposite effect and converts F26BP back to fructose-6-phosphate.  F26BP directly affects the following enzymes:

  • Stimulates phosphofructokinase-1, which catalyzes the rate-limiting step of glycolysis (fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate)

  • Inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, which catalyzes a key regulatory step of gluconeogenesis (fructose-1,6-bisphosphate → fructose-6-phosphate)

When F26BP levels are high, gluconeogenesis is inhibited, which decreases glucose production from precursors such as alanine.  Alanine is supplied to the liver via the glucose-alanine cycle, which helps maintain euglycemia during fasting.  Amino groups from skeletal muscle protein breakdown are transferred to pyruvate, forming alanine, which is released into the circulation.  In the liver, alanine aminotransferase converts alanine to pyruvate, which then enters gluconeogenesis.  Because carbon from alanine (as well as from lactate and glycerol) must pass through the fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase step to become glucose, high F26BP levels decrease the conversion of alanine to glucose, even though F26BP does not act on alanine aminotransferase itself.

(Choice A)  Fatty acid synthesis is upregulated by insulin and high citrate levels (citrate accumulates with active glycolysis and allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase).  Therefore, fatty acid synthesis typically increases when F26BP levels are high.

(Choice C)  The conversion of glucose to ribose-5-phosphate is carried out by the pentose phosphate pathway.  The pathway also produces NADPH, which is used for reductive biosynthesis (eg, fatty acid synthesis).  Its rate-limiting enzyme, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, is inhibited by NADPH and induced by insulin; it is not affected by F26BP levels.

(Choice D)  Glycogenesis is stimulated by increased levels of insulin and glucose-6-phosphate.  Because elevated insulin levels also increase F26BP formation, rising F26BP levels in hepatocytes are typically concurrent with increasing glycogen synthesis.

(Choice E)  The rise in F26BP accelerates glycolysis, leading to increased conversion of NAD+ to NADH at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step.

Educational objective:Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F26BP) activates phosphofructokinase-1, increasing glycolysis, and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, decreasing gluconeogenesis from substrates such as alanine, lactate, and glycerol.  The F26BP concentration is regulated by a bifunctional enzyme.  Insulin activates the kinase domain (phosphofructokinase-2), increasing F26BP, whereas glucagon activates the phosphatase domain (fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase), decreasing F26BP.​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌
